In this paper, we successfully propose a highly efficient linear, decoupled, fully
discrete, variable time step second-order backward difference formula (VBDF2)
finite element numerical scheme for the Cahn–Hilliard–Navier–Stokes (CHNS)
model. First, by utilizing the invariant energy quadratization (IEQ) method, we
derive the equivalent CHNS model, which is crucial for handling the nonlinear
terms. Second, by employing the finite element method for spatial discretiza-
tion and the VBDF2 approach for time discretization, we obtain the fully discrete
numerical scheme. Then, we also demonstrate the unique solvability, mass con-
servation property, and stability of the IEQ-VBDF2 scheme. Subsequently, we
present the error estimates accompanied by rigorous theoretical derivations.
Finally, we creatively design an adaptive variable-time-step strategy and con-
duct several numerical simulations to verify the theoretical results. This strategy
boasts excellent performance. It can maintain a high level of computational
accuracy while significantly enhancing computational efficiency, offering a more
efficient and reliable solution for the relevant numerical computing field.

INTRODUCTION
The Cahn–Hilliard–Navier–Stokes (CHNS) equation, which couples the Cahn–Hilliard (CH) and Navier–Stokes (NS)
equations, has significant research value in various fields, such as continuum mechanics and materials science. It can
describe interfacial changes and fluid motion [1, 2]. The CH equations, which are fourth-order nonlinear parabolic partial
differential equations, were first introduced by John W. Cahn and John E. Hilliard [3]. It describes the temporal evolution
of the order parameter (such as concentration) in an inhomogeneous system by minimizing the free energy of the system,
characterizing the processes of phase separation and interfacial dynamics. The NS equation was proposed by Claude-Louis
Navier and refined by George Gabriel Stokes [4, 5]. It describes the laws of motion for viscous Newtonian fluids.
The CHNS equations have been widely applied in many scientific and engineering fields, such as fluid mechanics and
materials science [3, 6]. A relatively straightforward application is in the field of fluid mechanics, such as the simulation
of bubble dynamics [7]. As for other applications, in the field of materials science, they can be used to study the solidi-
fication of liquid metal alloys [8] and the phase separation process of alloys, as well as to optimize material properties;
in biomedical engineering, they can simulate the fluid flow and material transport phenomena in living organisms [9],
providing theoretical support for medical diagnosis and treatment. In addition, this model can also assist in simulating
immiscible fluid systems containing colloids, and can be used to stabilize bicontinuous gels and design new soft materials
[10, 11]. For more detailed physical backgrounds and applications of the phase-field-Navier–Stokes equations, please refer
to refs. [12, 13] and the literature cited therein.

In recent years, the CHNS system has attracted widespread academic research attention. A large number of scholars
have dedicated themselves to developing diverse numerical solution methods for this system. For example, Shen and Li
[14] constructed a numerical scheme for the CHNS phase field model based on the scalar auxiliary variable (SAV) approach
in time and the MAC discretization in space. They demonstrated the energy stability of the system, established second-
order fully-discrete error estimates for the relevant variables, and verified the robustness and accuracy of the scheme
through numerical experiments. Chen and Yang [15] devised an effective fully discrete finite element numerical scheme.
They merged the penalty method of the NS equations with the Strang operator splitting approach and incorporated several
nonlocal variables along with their ordinary differential equations to address the coupled nonlinear terms. Additionally,
in ref. [16], they formulated a new fully decoupled numerical technique for the variable-density/viscosity CH phase field
model of the two-phase incompressible fluid flow system. This technique enables the explicit discretization of the nonlin-
ear coupling terms and ensures unconditional energy stability. Based on the projection method of the NS equation and the
stabilization of the CH equation, Chen et al. [17] developed a fully decoupled, linear finite element scheme that is uncon-
ditionally energy-stable. Moreover, they conducted an error analysis for this scheme. Recently, Chen et al. [18] proposed
several unconditional energy-stable IEQ finite element methods (FEMs) for the purpose of solving the CHNS equations.
For more details of the related studies, please refer to refs. [19–24].
According to the literature search, there are scarcely any studies on the error analysis of the variable time step second-
order backward difference formula (VBDF2) scheme for the CHNS system. Compared to the fixed time step, the coefficient
sequence of the variable time step is more complex, which increases the difficulty of theoretical analysis. However, the
variable time step method enables us to take larger time steps in the stable region compared to the fixed time step method.
This will significantly improve the computational efficiency without sacrificing the calculation accuracy. In recent years,
there have been some studies on the variable time step method. Based on second-order backward differences, the convex-
splitting technique, and viscous regularization at the discrete level, Chen et al. [25] proposed and analyzed a second-order
semi-discrete VBDF2 numerical scheme for the CH equation. In ref. [26], the authors proposed a series of implicit–explicit

When dealing with problems related to the CH equation, how to handle the nonlinear term 𝑓(𝜙) in the system has
always been a widely discussed issue in the industry. Common treatment methods include the SAV method [29, 36–39]
and the invariant energy quadratization (IEQ) method [40–42]. These two methods have been quite popular in recent
years. In addition, there are also some classic methods such as the convex splitting method [43] and the stabilized semi-
implicit method [44]. In addition, the computational efficiency of relevant numerical experiments is also a key point
that requires attention. Although the variable time step method can significantly improve computational efficiency, this
method also increases the difficulty of theoretical analysis. Therefore, most of the literature on the error analysis of (1.1)
focuses on the fixed time step.
In this paper, we propose a new, efficient, and high-precision IEQ-VBDF2 scheme for the CHNS model. First, we use
the IEQ method to handle the nonlinear terms in the model. This is because when dealing with nonlinear terms, the
IEQ method only requires a lower bound, is more flexible than traditional methods, and also has excellent computational
efficiency and outstanding scheme accuracy [40]. Second, we adopt the finite element method for spatial discretization
and the VBDF2 method for time discretization to obtain the fully discrete numerical scheme. We prove the unique solv-
ability, mass conservation property, and stability of the IEQ-VBDF2 scheme. We also provide an error estimate of this
scheme through strict theoretical derivations. Finally, we design an adaptive variable time step strategy and conduct
several numerical simulation experiments to verify our conclusions.
Subsequently, in the second part of this paper, we shall introduce some fundamental mathematical knowledge employed
herein, encompassing several definitions and theorems. In the third part, we will expound upon the specific form of the
CHNS equation under the IEQ method and demonstrate the energy dissipation law and mass conservation under this
scheme.In the fourth part, we formulate the IEQ-VBDF finite element scheme. Moreover, we prove the unique solvability,
mass conservation, and stability of this scheme. In the fifth part, we will derive the error estimate for this scheme. In the
sixth part, we devise an adaptive time-step strategy and present a number of numerical simulation experiments. Finally,
in the seventh part, we offer a summary of this paper.

adaptive time-stepping algorithm has been meticulously designed. The accuracy and effectiveness of this algorithm have
been rigorously verified through extensive numerical simulations. Our principal objective has been to derive the second-
